subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this legislation is an unnecessary, poorly drafted and thought-out amendment to the Canada Business Corporations Act. In 1975, after a great deal of discussion by the Canadian Bar Association and other people involved in business corporations, this House finally passed the Canada Business Corporations Act. That act was at least ten years in the drafting stage. That act made it easier for companies to raise money. It made it easier to incorporate companies. It gave minority shareholders, and shareholders generally, remedies against directors so that they could not be abused as they had been in the past. Generally speaking there was a modernization of our corporate law.
I want to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that act was thought out, drafted, and redrafted. It was presented as a comprehensive piece of legislation dealing with how we organize business corporations on a national basis. But this is an ill-conceived piece of legislation that is now presented to us as part of the national energy package.
Canada Business Corporations Act
I want to say to members of this House that while they may think they are passing a piece of legislation that has something to do with energy, this bill has absolutely nothing to do with national energy or energy policy. This bill allows changes in the basic structure of corporate law. It will seriously hurt the raising of capital on the stock markets. It will seriously hurt companies in all sorts of deals other than energy; in transportation; in banking; in trust companies; in the distribution of liquor or of beer. It will seriously hurt all sorts of activities yet to be devised, and perhaps land holdings. It will hurt the development of business in Canada and the raising of capital in Canada. The bill does not just apply to oil. It applies to any company where the laws of Canada, or any province, make it more advisable for a company to have shares held by Canadians. If the particular business in which the company is involved falls within that ambit and there is a prescription of that type of company, it can take advantage of the provisions of this act.
Briefly, its provisions provide that a company can first deal in its own shares by buying shares on the stock market and reselling them, allegedly to Canadianize itself. Or a company can do one thing further. It can issue shares that are constrained with respect to ownership. It can then sell those shares and, at some future date, call in those shares in proportion as it feels best. It can take the shares of people who may not be Canadian that are allegedly constrained and it can sell those shares for what can be obtained on the marketplace, giving those shareholders who happen to be investors in Canadian corporations the net proceeds from the sale of that stock.
The bill demonstrates a complete lack of understanding of how the market system works. I want to deal with the issues in the bill as two separate portions and how those issues affect the entirety of corporate law in the country. The first portion of the bill, Clause 2, deals with the situation where a board of directors finds that it would be advantageous to a company to be Canadian, so to speak, gets designated in that fashion by the minister, then goes into the market, purchases its own shares and resells them. In other words, the company wheels and deals its own shares.
When the Canada Business Corporations Act was passed in 1975, for the first time in our corporate history we gave companies the right to be able to buy their own shares as an investment. That gave companies in Canada a great deal of flexibility. It meant that they could buy out shareholders and pay them off for their share of the equity in companies. We must remember when looking at the ownership of a company that the equity in a company is basically held by the common shareholders. They may not be common shareholders, but equity shareholders of some kind, some of whom may or may not have a vote. But the equity in a company is what we will call for argument's sake the common shareholders' share. That equity represents what was originally subscribed for the shares in the first place from treasury together with the built-up profits or surplus, after tax, reflected in the corporate balance

May 18, 1982
Canada Business Corporations Act
sheet. By dividing the equity among the shareholders, you find out the book value of what each share is worth. If there is a reduction in the number of shares by the company buying some of its own shares, then there is no damage to the balance of the remaining shareholders. However, if we allow that to take place, there is no damage and it is good for business.
But what we have here is a situation where the officers and directors of a corporation are entitled by the provisions of this bill to go to the marketplace, buy up shares with the treasury of the company, using all shareholders' money, but instead of leaving the benefit to the remaining shareholders as is presently the law, turning around and giving that benefit away to whomever they wish in any kind of a deal they wish, as long as they stay within the purposes of Section 31(1), which presumably is to increase Canadianization of a particular company.
I say to you, Sir, if we were really necessarily Canadianizing companies this way, some people in an ultranationalistic fashion might say that is appropriate. But what happens and what is contemplated under the statute is that shares openly traded on the market might be purchased by the company without notification-because there is no provision for notification in the act-and sold out to someone else. In other words, the shareholders' money, the equity in the company, can be used by the directors in the company to speculate in its own stock to buy and sell that stock. In the name of Canadianization, it is an open door for scoundrels to wheel and deal at tlje expense of shareholders. Indeed, the wheeling and dealing can take place at the expense of Canadian shareholders, not just of foreign shareholders.
May I remind you that in an open market situation, in the average well-traded corporation, the majority of shares are held by people who have no intention-certainly for some considerable period of time-of trading those shares. Under normal conditions it is easy to determine the ownership or the citizenship of those shares. But some of the shares represent shares which are often held in the hands of brokers in street form. Those are the shares on which the day-to-day trade back and forth determines the market value listed in the daily newspapers.
Now, what has happened? Under this bill the corporation is entitled, if it is prescribed, to go into the marketplace to wheel and deal in the trading of shares of the company. The corporation does not know, when it wheels and deals, whether the shares are held for Mr. Speaker, for example, in his broker's name. They could be held for Mr. Speaker in his broker's name in street form so that they can be easily transferred- and he is a Canadian-or they could be held for someone else in the broker's name. Who knows whose shares are whose? Shares in that form do not carry a passport or a birth certificate. They are shares which are open and being traded. Some of them may be held that way for weeks, for months or indeed for years. Some of them may be traded overnight or day to day. They never hit the registry again until someone says to the broker: "I want them registered in my name." Then one might be able to find out who is the citizen; but until that occurs one has no idea who the citizen is who owns the shares.
The government, the minister and his departmental officials have some idea that market shares held in street form should carry a passport with them. The clear indication in any market is that they do not. The only company mentioned in the public hearings which could even possibly want this legislation was Dome Petroleum. When its directors decide to go into the marketplace, they might buy Mr. Speaker's shares, the shares of some other member or the shares of a foreigner. It would not matter whether they bought in New York, Toronto or Vancouver because they would not know whose shares they were buying. When, Mr. Speaker, you buy a share in the stock market, you do not know whether you are buying a Canadian, an American or a Greek share. You buy a share, you pay the market price and you pay the broker's fee. In effect, this bill will allow the company to use corporate money which belongs to shareholders allegedly to Canadianize and to go into the open market to buy shares. I say that they could well be buying only Canadian shares and that only Canadians will be defrauded by the misuse of the equity in their company.
Does the minister pay attention to that? No, he is so set in his ways to get this bill through that he refuses to take a look at what the bar, the stockmarket, or life insurance companies and pension funds say on the matter. He says, "I am going to Canadianize." Somehow he now wants to go one step further and change basic corporate law. In committee we pointed out to the minister that it would be very simple, if he wanted, to provide for a company to make a general offering to foreign shareholders to purchase their shares at a specified offer or tender form. That would reduce foreign shareholdings and that would be fair. Foreign shareholders could take their shares and tender them to the company for transfer or cancellation. We would know that we were buying foreign shares at the offered price. The minister would have none of that because presumably it would mess up the trading activities he had in mind. One wonders whether the minister really has Canadianization in mind or whether it will be an opportunity for those who are directors of energy corporations or other corporations, where some conceivable benefit might be available from Canadian ownership, to wheel and deal in the marketplace. This wheeling and dealing in the marketplace concerns us a great deal.
We are a country which needs to raise equity capital, not just from Canadians but from anywhere we can. We are talking about raising risk capital for risk investments. We must ensure that our market is as broad, fair, honest and straightforward as possible. When we allow a situation to exist where it is possible under our corporate law for a shareholder somehow to be diddled by the directors of the corporation, when there is a fear that he could be diddled or bought out with his own money and not know it, we put into the investment climate of the country uncertainty and a feeling that perhaps the game is not fair or honest.
I say to hon. members on the government benches-and there are few of them here-that this is a piece of legislation which should not be passed. When I asked the minister and his
May 18, 1982

officials in committee who made representations to them and said that they needed this piece of legislation to Canadianize the oil industry, they could not answer. Finally, at the last meeting of the committee before the bill was rammed through with the usual government majority-ready, aye, ready-they told me as the member of the official opposition who was there-and no member of the New Democratic Party bothered to come-that they could only find one company which made representations, Dome Petroleum. They said that maybe it would affect Norcen, that maybe Norcen could take advantage of it, but that Dome Petroleum could use it. I think the bill should really be amended to read, "An Act to amend the Business Corporations Act for Dome Petroleum Limited or Dome Resources". We could call it the Dome bill. When the basic corporate law is changed because of the representation of one widely-held energy corporation that might like to Canadianize or might do better if it could Canadianize in full, there is something wrong.
I should like to go on to other portions of the bill which do not necessarily deal with the business of wheeling and dealing in stock but deal with another serious issue, and that is the issue of constrained shares. The bill, in its amendments to the act, provides that a corporation can issue classes of constrained shares, constrained as to ownership. I have no objection to that other than the fact that if shares are constrained as to ownership, 1 am not at all sure that we have not somewhere along the line breached the recently passed Charter of Rights and Freedoms contained in the Constitution. Surely the constraint we are talking about here is not that of preventing non-citizens from owning shares. It constrains Canadians, because the concept of "constraint" is Canadians who happen to be citizens of this country or landed immigrants living in this country.
What happens if you are a Canadian citizen posted abroad with our armed forces, or posted abroad in the foreign service, or a Canadian working for Petro-Canada International off the coast of China where we are drilling oil wells? In those cases you have broken the constraint. You are not a Canadian any more! Another example is those Canadians who have retired after working hard in this country for all their working lives and have moved to a warmer climate. They are no longer Canadian.
When asked about that the minister said that there are people who take their shares out of the country because they do not want to pay taxes in Canada. So he concludes that if you do not live in the country you cannot own oil company shares because those oil companies could get the advantage of PIP grants. What kind of minister, what kind of party, what kind of government is it that tells Canadians that they are no longer Canadians at some point but are relegated to second class because they have retired to Florida or the Bahamas? What kind of government is it that tells a person he is not Canadian any more because he is asthmatic and had to move to Arizona? Because a person works for the Government of Canada in an embassy or trade commission abroad, he is not a Canadian any more. Or since a person is a member of our Armed Forces in Europe, he is no longer a Canadian according
Canada Business Corporations Act
to these statutes. That is the effect of this act on those Canadians. This is what the government is supporting.
Let us consider further the question of constrained shares. These shares can be constrained in regard to what kind of Canadian is resident in Canada, but for some strange reason they can be bought and held by people who are not Canadians resident in Canada. The exception is that if a Canadian should ever move out of the country, or if a foreigner should ever acquire shares, there is provision in the bill whereby the directors have the option to select any particular owner of these constrained shares and take the shares from some but not from others, sell the shares and give the owner the net proceeds. That shareholder does not receive what the shares are worth but only the net proceeds. In addition, this does not apply to every person who holds constrained shares but only to those who the company wants to place that constraint on. In other words, if you are a Canadian who lives outside the country the government might not acquire your shares but could take someone else's. If you have a friend who is on the board, you may be able to hold on to these constrained shares while living outside the country. However, someone else might end up being expropriated in the worst possible way. That is, the company takes your shares and after it deducts whatever it costs for their sale, seizure or trusteeship, you receive whatever proceeds are left.
The reason the legislation is written in this manner is due to poor draftsmanship. The law was intended to be much more serious to enable the company to deal with any class of shares. The intention was that the company could constrain shares after they were issued and do it all over again. However, the act was amended in that respect. All the other cumbersome clauses dealing with trusteeship, seizure of some shares and not others, and the sale and payment of net receipts were left in. When we asked the officials and the minister why these provisions remained unchanged, we did not get an answer in committee. The minister and the officials did not know the answer, though I suppose Dome Petroleum did not know the answer.
This statute which we are discussing is being presented as an energy bill. Members of the official opposition are told that the only company which ever made representations with respect to some changes in the Canada Business Corporations Act was Dome Petroleum. The act deals with more than just the oil and gas industry. It affects anyone with respect to any federal or provincial laws who wish to receive licences, permits, grants, payments or benefits by reason of obtaining and maintaining a specified level of Canadian ownership or control. This is a poor piece of legislation and this House will be doing a great disservice to Canada, to corporate law, to the development of our resources and the development of equity markets in our country if it is passed.

Therefore, in relation to this bill, I speak of the frustration I am sure many people across Canada feel with regard to the old forms and rules under which we are operating.

I know that the docket is fairly full now. There are many items on the Order Paper with which we should be dealing as they are important to the wellbeing of our economy and to our country as a whole. I do not want to dwell on that subject because it is not the subject of debate this evening, which is Bill C-105, dealing with the Canada Business Corporations Act. As I understand it, it is a bill which encourages Canadian investment in the energy industry. That is a laudable cause. There should be more Canadian investment in all sectors of the Canadian economy. We have been dependent for far too long upon the policies, economies and whims of other countries. Small things affecting other countries sometimes carry over into Canada.
I feel that if we had more control over our own destiny through parliamentary reform and also over our own economy through greater Canadian ownership, we would be all the better for it. I often think of Canadian ownership in the same light as the Potash Corporation in the province of Saskatchewan. The Potash Corporation of Saskatchewan was formed some years ago, in the early 1970s when the NDP government defeated Ross Thatcher's government. The idea came into being that we should have more control over our own resources. Part of the reason for this wish was the fact that in 1971, the last year of the Liberal administration in the province of Saskatchewan, we took in something like $14.7 million in resource revenues. I stand to be corrected on the figure, but it is fairly close. The people of the province of Saskatchewan said; "That is not adequate; we do not think the holders of the resources in this province are paying their fair share to the people of Saskatchewan and we would like to see this situation changed." The newly elected NDP government in Saskatchewan went to the potash corporations and said, "We will increase the rate of taxation against your industry in the province of Saskatchewan". Some of the potash corporations, all of the privately-owned ones, said, "We think the tax is a little unreasonable. It is much higher than we have previously been paying, but we are willing to pay that to the province of Saskatchewan because we enjoy operating in the province. You have a commodity that is of interest to us and we can resell it at a profit, so we will pay that higher rate of taxation and remain in the province of Saskatchewan."
However, in the meantime there were other potash companies in the province of Saskatchewan which said: "That rate is unfair and we will not pay the new increased rate of taxation; we will refuse to pay it." The province of Saskatchewan replied, "Well, that is fine. We think we represent the people of Saskatchewan with a fairly strong mandate and we think the taxation rate is fair. However, if you open up your books to us and show us that you are not making a good profit, a good return on your investment, then we are willing to reduce that rate of taxation." Some of the companies opened their books to the province and showed the returns they were making, not only in their own company but sometimes in their mother company, which might be in Pittsburgh, or in Johannesburg, South Africa. Many of the potash company owners, in the early years before the Potash Corporation of Saskatchewan came along, were owned by foreign investors.

This speaks to the point of Bill C-105, which is to encourage Canadian investment. We needed that. However, other companies would not open up their books at that time in Saskatchewan. Accordingly, the Potash Corporation of Saskatchewan was set up as a publicly-owned Crown corporation. This illustration extends beyond the boundaries of Saskatchewan. It could have been Canadian people investing in Canadian business; it does not have to be on a provincial scale. However, through the Potash Corporation of Saskatchewan, the people of Saskatchewan invested in the potash resource there.
As someone who has been involved in small business, I would not have minded had some private investors from Saskatchewan bought into some of those potash companies. But for the life of me, I cannot find that there were people in Saskatchewan with the millions of dollars in venture capital it would have taken to go into the potash mines. I therefore thought to myself that it was better that the people of Saskatchewan owned the resource than some outside interests from the United States, South Africa or other countries throughout the world. In Saskatchewan there were not the private investors with the kind of capital necessary to invest in some of the potash companies. Some of the small business people could not form together as co-operatives. Even the larger businesses in that province could not. I say that it holds true throughout the country that there was not enough capital to go into that industry.
When the Potash Corporation was set up, its objective was to buy the controlling interest in potash production in the province. It succeeded in that objective. But the beauty of the potash industry is that not only is it a publicly-owned Crown corporation, the Potash Corporation of Saskatchewan, based on the profit motive for the people of that province, but there are also privately-owned corporations still mining potash in the province. 1 think of Noranda, Central Canada Potash and Kalium Chemicals between Moose Jaw and Regina. These companies are happy to be private sector investors in the potash industry in Saskatchewan, which will continue to expand the economy for many years to come.
It remains to be seen what will happen with the new government, whether it will retain that very valuable Crown corporation or sell it off to the private sector. I think the new government will likely keep that Crown corporation. It brings a great deal of money into the coffers of the province of Saskatchewan. As a result, the many social programs there do not have to be taxed directly to the people and taken out of their pockets. Every year the potash corporation puts a great deal of money into the provincial coffers. I would speculate that the new Saskatchewan Conservative government, which, having been democratically elected and having majority in that province, deserves to be given a chance, will not sell that Crown corporation because of the benefit it gives to the people of that province.
As I said earlier, the resource funds which flowed into the provincial coffers in 1971 amounted to $14.7 million. That was under a Liberal administration. Some ten short years later, an
Canada Business Corporations Act
NDP administration under the very capable and undisputed leadership of Allan Blakeney was able to turn around that resource revenue to the point that in 1981 the province of Saskatchewan received $1 billion in resource revenue. That is one thousand million dollars in 1981 under an NDP administration compared to $14.7 million ten years previous under a Liberal administration.
Bill C-105, which encourages Canadians to invest in the energy industry, is good because of the fact that it encourages Canadians to invest. However, we do not believe that Bill C-105 will accomplish that. We think that such things as the resource sector should be heavily owned by the public sector and should have the strongest interest of Canadians at heart. Resources, whether it be energy, hydrocarbons, potash or any other non-renewable resource, will not be there forever.
The interests of the Canadian people who own the resources should be protected. We in the NDP believe that people within a province or country own the resources that are upon or beneath their soil. To keep something that is not renewable in the best interests of the people, there must be very heavy public sector involvement. The profit motive, which most Canadians have because they want to feed their families and provide them with a good lifestyle in appreciation of the high standard of living we have had and want to continue to have, requires public sector involvement to ensure that it is good for all people in the country.
We in the New Democratic Party feel that over the years the Liberal Party and Conservative Party have not had the best interests of Canadians at heart. I do not say the Liberals and Conservatives are not interested in the Canadian people, I believe they are; but the route they are taking is the wrong one. I do not think private sector involvement alone in the energy industry or with regard to any non-renewable resource is in the best interest of the Canadian people.
We in the New Democratic Party intend to vote against Bill C-105 because it is not going to benefit Canadians as a whole. We would like to see Canada prosper more than it is now.
We have what is even worse than a stagnant economy. It is going downhill every day. One need only watch the news reports each evening. If it is not the disastrous world situation where people are afraid of a nuclear holocaust or another world war breaking out, it is the disastrous economic condition of our country. We have an abundance of natural resources and well-trained people in terms of our academic and technical skills. We have come too far to give away what we now have.
I thank the House for listening to my input in this debate. I believe that Canadians will gain further through public sector involvement in the resource industries of this country. We should have a public sector involvement which will guard the interests of Canadian people.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I think it is germane for me to spend a few minutes discussing this, because I consider this the single, most important amendment to this bill that will be dealt with in the discussion of Bill C-102.
The amendments that we will be moving on this side to this bill are not to be deemed, even if they pass, as to warrant support by this party and this House for the bill. The amendments we are proposing tonight are simply a means of damage control, of trying to limit the amount of damage that is being done to the public interest by the bill before us. Let us make no mistake about it; it is a bad bill. It is a bill that does not deserve the support of the members of the House of Commons. It is a bill that is injurious to the interests of the people of Canada.
In no area is this bill a worse bill than the provision in the bill that would automatically accord agent of Her Majesty status to all new Crown corporations incorporated under this legislation. I am delighted that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) is here tonight, because it is the President of the Treasury Board who has the responsibility in government for drawing up comprehensive Crown corporation policy. It is very important that he participate in this debate as well to explain his position as President of the Treasury Board and whether he believes that automatically all new Crown corporations incorporated under this bill should be given special privileges.

May 18, 1982
Energy, Mines and Resources
The privileges which would come from this provision are very significant ones. Most Canadians are not aware of what "agent of Her Majesty" means. It is an expression which appears very Archaean and innocuous, but it conveys very significant privileges.
Perhaps the best way for me to explain to members of the House is to refer them to the uranium cartel case which is currently before the courts. I will not comment on the merits of the case. Hon. members on this side of the House have raised them on a number of occasions, but suffice it to say that the government finally agreed that a number of uranium companies should be charged with price-fixing for contravening the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act. That is a criminal offence, and the case included both private sector companies and two companies which were owned by the Government of Canada. One of them was Eldorado Nuclear, and the other was Uranium Canada.
When that matter came before the courts, the two Crown corporations pleaded in their case that they could not be charged because, as agents of Her Majesty, they were immune from the criminal law. Indeed, in a decision made by the Ontario Supreme Court on this case, the court found as follows:
It is clear that the long-standing historical immunity of the Crown or its agent is not to be lightly dispensed with. Section 16 of the Interpretation Act was in force before the commencement of the period specified in the charge, prior to the incorporation of U.C. and prior to the inclusion of Eldorado under the protection granted by section 3 of the Government Companies Act. Whatever the intention of Parliament relating to the application of the Combines Investigation Act to these companies, adequate time has expired to permit this to be done. Nothing has been done and at present there is no language in the Combines Investigation Act which purports to make that statute binding upon Her Majesty or to affect Her Majesty's rights or prerogatives in any manner. The language of section 16 is, on the other hand, clear and unambiguous. (See The Canadian Broadcasting Company and The Attorney-General for Ontario, supra, particularly the judgment of Rand J. at pages 198 and 199).
The judge said:
In my opinion then, section 16 is a complete answer to all submissions made by the Attorney General here, and I find that the Combines Investigation Act is not binding upon either of the applicants. In this regard, the conduct complained of in these charges, assuming it is capable of proof, cannot be characterized as criminal and there exists no foundation upon which these charges could be validly laid or prosecuted under the Combines Investigation Act.
What does this mean? This means that when the government includes a provision for automatically granting agent of Her Majesty status to these Crown corporations, it sets two standards. There is one standard for the private sector and for all ordinary Canadians and another standard entirely for the government. It says that federal corporations which operate as agents of Her Majesty are above the combines law and that they can engage in price-fixing. They can engage in the sort of manipulation which would lead to charges being laid in the private sector. In other instances they could engage in false and misleading advertising. A Crown corporation can be exempt from prosecution under statutes dealing with false and
misleading advertising. They can be immune from other criminal prosecution as agents of Her Majesty.
It is intolerable to any Member of Parliament who is concerned about respect for the rule of law to accept a situation whereby automatically all new Crown corporations incorporated under this bill would automatically be given that immunity. There must be one standard of law in Canada, and if the government chooses to put in place combines legislation designed to ensure that price fixing does not exist, designed to ensure that one cannot engage in false and misleading advertising and designed to ensure that practices in the marketplace are fair and scrupulous, how can it with any justification seek to exempt its own companies from maintaining the same standards of behaviour we would expect of private sector companies? If private sector companies violate the Combines Investigation Act or if they violate other criminal legislation, charges are laid against them and they are prosecuted in the courts. Yet what we find in the Eldorado and Uranium Canada case is that the government using the fact that the two Crown corporations were agents of Her Majesty, and the corporations have declared themselves immune from the application of the criminal law.

For that reason alone it would be wrong automatically to confer agent of Her Majesty status in these instances on these companies which, by and large, will be operating as competitors in the marketplace. However, the privileges and immunities which are conferred by the granting of agent of Her Majesty status goes well beyond simply the ability to thumb one's nose at the Combines Investigation Act.
Equally important and equally odious is the fact that these companies operating in the marketplace would not raise money on their own credit rating. They would not have to establish that they were credit worthy, that they were well managed, that they were good companies or that they were worthy companies to which to lend money. When an agent of Her Majesty enters into markets and tries to raise money, an agent of Her Majesty does so with the credit rating of the Government of Canada. That means these companies automatically have a triple A credit rating. Their competitors in the marketplace have to raise money on the basis of their own credit rating. These Crown corporations, being granted agent of Her Majesty status, will automatically be able to do so with the best terms possible, that is, the best commercial terms available to the Government of Canada.
It goes one step beyond that. In cases where these companies are ill-managed and where ultimately we find they go bankrupt and there are massive losses incurred, as was the case with Consolidated Computer in which $125 million was poured down the drain, what happens in the case of an agent of Her Majesty? In a case where an agent of Her Majesty has incurred debts and goes bankrupt, those debts are automatically charges upon the consolidated revenue fund of Canada. Parliament does not have any discretion in a case like that. The people of Canada, the taxpayers of Canada, are automatically responsible for any debts which are incurred by these Crown corporations.
No one knows-and if the President of the Treasury Board in any way disputes this, I invite him to participate in the debate-what the potential liability of agents of Her Majesty is or how much the taxpayers of Canada could ultimately be charged for mismanagement by Crown corporations which are agents of Her Majesty. Nor do we know when we are asked to pass this legislation tonight how many Crown corporations will be created, what will be their scope, what will be their size and what sort of debts they will be running up for which the taxpayers of Canada would be responsible. If tonight we grant automatic agent of Her Majesty status, we will be giving an unlimited credit card drawn on the account of the people of Canada to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) to be used by any new Crown corporation in the energy field which he chooses to set up. How could members of this House of Commons do that? How could anyone who witnessed the fiasco of the Consolidated Computer case and the loss of $125 million because of the negligence of the President of the Treasury Board and his colleagues accept that as a practice which would be tolerable for Members of Parliament? Clearly we have a responsibility on us, and clearly the President of the Treasury Board has a direct responsibility on him, to ensure that we do not give this unlimited ability to
Energy, Mines and Resources
Crown corporations to run up debts on behalf of the people of Canada beyond the control of Parliament.
I should make one thing clear, and that is that the government already has the capability through other legislation to confer agent of Her Majesty status on any Crown corporation it chooses. The government can do that today. The issue is not whether in some instances it will be appropriate in the future to confer agent of Her Majesty status on some Crown corporations. The issue is whether Parliament today should be saying for all time that all Crown corporations created under this legislation will automatically be given agent of Her Majesty status. By doing so we will automatically be granting them immunity from combines investigation legislation, will automatically be granting them immunity from some taxes and will automatically be giving them privileges in terms of raising money that their competitors do not have. They will automatically be able to borrow on the government's credit rating and to hold the taxpayers of Canada responsible for their debts, if they are ill-managed.
If the hon. member for Regina West is prepared to do some homework, I would invite him to consider the reports of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts on Crown corporations. That committee found that it was essential to bring some control and accountability to Crown corporations. This was after a succession of scandals during the sixties and seventies that involved Crown corporations and the misuse of public funds. I would invite him to look into the Estey report on Air Canada which found there were inadequate controls on these Crown corporations. I would invite him to look at the report of the Lambert Royal Commission on Financial Management and Accountability which recommended that controls be put in place. 1 would invite him to read the successive reports of the Auditor General of Canada to Parliament which said it was essential to bring in legislation that would ensure that the taxpayers of Canada are protected and that the sort of fiascos that occur when Crown corporations run up unlimited bills and pick the pocket of the taxpayer to pay for them could not happen in the future.
These are not partisan authorities, Mr. Speaker. The public accounts committee represents all parties in this House, and the Auditor General of Canada, a royal commission and a judicial inquiry have some standing. The hon. member for Regina West may scoff at those authorities, but there are some members in this House, Mr. Speaker, who believe they have a responsibility to the taxpayers of Canada. There are some who believe that when they are dealing with billions of dollars they have a responsibility as custodians to ensure that the money is well spent and is not simply poured down the drain.
I have constituents who are smarting because of the present financial situation, who desperately need the money that is being taken from them in taxes, who need assistance from the government. If money is not available to my farmers in the form of assistance but is poured down the drain because of the

May 18, 1982
Energy, Mines and Resources
mismanagement of a Crown corporation which has been granted agent of Tier Majesty status, then I have not done my job as a Member of Parliament.
If constituents of the hon. member for Regina West who are having a hard time paying their mortgages, who find there is no assistance available to them from the government, are being forced to pay taxes as a result of the mismanagement of Crown corporations because the hon. member has decided that the liabilities of Crown corporations automatically become liabilities of his constituents, then I say he is not doing his job either.
I will return to my first point, Mr. Speaker. Even if it were not enough that Parliament had a responsibility to exercise some prudence and to show some concern about the management of the moneys we hold in trust for the people of Canada, surely when the Canadian people are beginning to lose respect for their institutions and when respect for the rule of law is being lost, the government should act to restore respect for the rule of law. It should not take actions which would create a new group of companies operating in the marketplace which would be immune to criminal legislation and would be able to take the law into their own hands and disregard law passed by Parliament to protect consumers.
This is not the time to slacken laws; it is the time to ensure that the government meets the most stringent standards and sets an example that can be respected by the people of Canada.
At the present time some 50 Crown corporations operate in the marketplace as agents of Her Majesty. This bill would give the government authority to incorporate an unlimited number of new Crown corporations, every one of which would automatically be agents of Her Majesty.
To go a step further, because they would be incorporated under the Canada Business Corporations Act, these corporations would have the ability to incorporate subsidiaries and those subsidiaries yet further subsidiaries in Canada and outside Canada, under federal companies legislation, under provincial companies legislation, and under international legislation. All of these would automatically be agents of Her Majesty and would automatically have the ability to stick the Canadian taxpayer with any bill incurred because of mismanagement.
There have been a number of instances where mismanagement has existed.

FINANCE-PROJECTED BUDGET DEFICIT. (B) FOREIGN AID EXPENDITURES-REQUEST FOR REFERRAL TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday I had the occasion to ask two questions of the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres). The first dealt with the serious deteriorating nature of our current deficit. I made reference to the fact that the deficit was originally projected six months ago to stand in the amount of $10.49 billion. I asked the Minister of State for Finance whether the Department of Finance had prepared new projections as to what the deficit for the current year would be. The question was founded upon the presumption, logically arrived at, that having regard to the massively increased costs incurred by the government as a consequence

May 18, 1982
Adjournment Debate
of the failing economy and the known reduction in revenues generated, it was anticipated that the deficit would increase and increase substantially.
The uncertainty as to the quantum of that increase, however, has led in my view to a serious undermining of the value of our currency. That decline has been rectified in part by the traditional practice followed by this government of shoring up the value of our dollar by increasing interest rates in Canada using the agency of the Bank of Canada. The increase in interest rates has triggered a negative response to the government's alleged attack on inflation, the declared enemy. At the same time it has forced more businesses out of business and it has exacerbated the amount of unemployment suffered in the country. Currently we have at least 1.5 million working Canadians who are no longer working as a result of this foolhardy policy adopted by the current government.
It seems appropriate, in the event the decline of our dollar with all of the consequential effects to which I have made reference is to be stemmed, for the government to disclose a new set of financial figures indicating exactly the nature of the deficit that we may anticipate for the current year.
The government's response to this significant issue has been to lay blame for our economic plight upon the government of the United States. I pause to ask if, indeed, our entire financial position as a nation is to be determined by actions of another government, why do we need a Minister of Finance? Why do we need a Department of Finance and why do we need a Minister of State for Finance if all they can do is come into this House and explain to the people of Canada that we must await some measure of improvement to come from a foreign country.
If I had any doubt as to the need for the Minister of State for Finance, that doubt was rather rapidly resolved by his response to my second question. I asked, in light of current economic circumstances in this country, whether it would not be appropriate, having regard to our massive foreign aid program which currently in terms of direct funding exceeds $1,724 million, to refer the issue of the quantum of foreign aid to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence for examination. The minister's response to me was as follows:
Madam Speaker, perhaps the hon. member could stop staring at his navel-
1 asked that question in all seriousness.
I am not familiar with the constituency represented by the Minister of State for Finance, but I can tell the House that somewhere within his constituency there are some of those businesses which have gone bankrupt that are represented by the 39 per cent increase in insolvencies in the country in the first quarter of this year over last year. Somewhere in his constituency there are farmers who have become insolvent and are represented by the 70 per cent increase in farm bankruptcies. Somewhere in his constituency there are some of those unemployed persons who are now forming an army.
Canadians are angry, and I am angry, with the flippant, arrogant response which the minister presented to me and to the House. Surely it is time that the government came to recognize that the people of Canada will no longer accept this kind of abuse. The government must begin to have some regard for the welfare of the people of Canada and adopt policies-if not this one, then surely some other-which will bring some relief to hard-pressed citizens of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE-PROJECTED BUDGET DEFICIT. (B) FOREIGN AID EXPENDITURES-REQUEST FOR REFERRAL TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I had an opportunity to visit the Caribbean Development Bank, an institution which serves the small islands running through the Caribbean Commonwealth area, the areas we think of whenever we think about a Caribbean vacation in the middle of the winter. All through that area, Canada has contributed magnificently in very practical ways to schools, fishery projects, forestry projects, airports and in a myriad of practical ways which enormously help the people in those countries. We are proud of our contributions in that area. I saw them with my own eyes. I saw how those projects improved the standard of living of those people. But I also saw, which the hon. member for York North (Mr. Gamble) will never admit, how those projects improved Canada's reputation abroad, improved our trade and how, in turn, they improved the ability of the people in those areas to rely on their own capacity and their own strength. We can be proud of those kinds of contributions. Those are the ideals which many of us who look higher than our navel will find are possible in the world.
The hon. member for York North plays on the opposite. He plays on the stingy and mean-mindedness in all of us. He tries to drag us down to a small ideal. He implies that we are all suffering some kind of enormous economic damage because of an act of generosity to other people around the world. His comments tonight carry these ideals to an extreme. He is telling us that building schools, airport hangars and forestry projects are leading to business and farm bankruptcies. The hon. member claims to be a practical man. He should in fact try that claim out on a few of his constituents, where he would be laughed out of the hall.
Let me give one simple example. Canada has said that it will increase its official development assistance to other countries to 0.5 per cent of our gross national product, hardly an extreme case, hardly an excess which will lead to suffering or damage in the economy. Instead, it is a universally recognized, humanitarian level which also helps our businesses, our selfreliance and our trade patterns around the world. We benefit as much as the people who receive this money.
As a final note, I will tell the House that when I listened to the people at the Caribbean Development Bank talking about the money we were using in that bank, they talked about good management, good project evaluation, increased purchases from Canada, streamlined loan administration and constant management review, ideals which I support.
